extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, students, and interested lay readers
extracted.subtask_description: A catalog of special claim forms and claim-drafting styles found in patent applications, with explanations of their legal features, examples, relevant case law, and jurisdictional practice differences. Useful for understanding drafting options and limits (e.g., what is allowed in the US vs. EPO/UK).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauregard claim
rubrics_metrics.description: In United States patent law, a Beauregard claim is a claim to a computer program written in the form of a claim to an article of manufacture: a computer‑readable medium on which are encoded, typically, instructions for carrying out a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains history and uncertainty: originated in In re Beauregard (1995). Historically faced the 'printed matter' doctrine; practice evolved to recite 'non‑transitory' computer‑readable media after In re Nuijten. Supreme Court decisions (e.g., Alice) and Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., CyberSource) can make Beauregard claims unpatentable if the underlying method is not patent‑eligible. EPO and UK practice differ (EPO allows computer program claim forms; UK practice has shifted with case law). Also notes practical decline in use as distribution moved from physical media to network delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhausted‑combination claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An exhausted‑combination claim comprises a claim (usually a machine claim) in which a novel device is combined with conventional elements in a conventional manner (e.g., a conventional PC containing a novel microprocessor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses doctrinal status (Federal Circuit held doctrine outdated in 1984) but notes potential practical significance for royalty base and exhaustion issues (Quanta assumed older precedents). Embedding a non‑satisfying machine‑or‑transformation element in a combination may be used tactically to appear to meet that test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional (means‑plus‑function / step‑plus‑function) claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional claim expresses a technical feature in functional terms (e.g., 'means for converting a digital electric signal into an analog electric signal' or 'step for converting...') and is governed by statutes and case law of the filing jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S., governed by 35 U.S.C. §112, paragraph 6: such claim elements are construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. Extensive analysis and complex case law exist; scope is limited to disclosed corresponding structure. Practitioners still use this style when the specification supports it, but it requires careful support in the specification and carries interpretive limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson claim
rubrics_metrics.description: In U.S. practice, a Jepson claim is a method or product claim where one or more limitations are specifically identified as a point of novelty, distinguishable over at least the contents of the preamble (e.g., '...wherein the improvement comprises:').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to call examiner's attention to a point of novelty without argument or amendment; was used to avoid double patenting in some contexts. But Jepson claims plainly admit that the preamble subject matter is prior art, which can facilitate obviousness arguments under 35 U.S.C. §103; thus they are seldom used in modern U.S. practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim / Markush structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainly used in chemistry: a Markush claim or structure is a claim with multiple 'functionally equivalent' chemical entities allowed in one or more parts of the compound (format often 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to claim alternatives/groups of chemical constituents considered equivalent for the invention. Can result in a very large number of possible compounds, creating searching/indexing challenges; specialized databases are used to search Markush structures. USPTO prescribes the proper format ('selected from the group consisting of A, B and C'). Regulatory/proposed changes to use of Markush claims have been considered historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A so‑called omnibus claim is a claim including a reference to the description or drawings without stating explicitly any technical features of the product or process claimed (e.g., 'The invention substantially as herein described').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European Patent Convention allows omnibus claims only 'when they are absolutely necessary'; UK practice has changed to disallow in most cases. Under U.S. law, omnibus claims are categorically disallowed in utility patents and are rejected as failing to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' subject matter required by 35 U.S.C. §112 paragraph 2. Design and plant patents typically have a single omnibus‑style claim by statute ('the ornamental design as shown in Figure 1').

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A product‑by‑process claim is directed to a product defined by its process of preparation (e.g., 'Product obtained by the process of claim X').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO practice: interpret as 'Product obtainable by the process of claim...' and permissible only if the product is patentable as such and cannot be sufficiently defined by composition/structure or other testable parameters. In the U.S., PTO practice has allowed product‑by‑process claims even for products that can be sufficiently described, but case law (e.g., Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz, 2009) makes such claims disadvantageous: to prove infringement the patentee must show both product and process elements, while invalidation may rely only on product elements in prior art. Distinguish protection conferred from pure process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmed computer claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A programmed computer claim is in the form 'a general‑purpose digital computer programmed to carry out [steps]' — the theory being that a new program makes an old general‑purpose computer into a new and different machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to avoid case law holding certain methods patent‑ineligible. Critics argue that loading a program into an old machine is analogous to putting a new piano roll into an old player piano (the 'piano roll blues' argument) and may not create a patentable machine; case law and statutory eligibility (e.g., Alice) affect viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach‑through claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A reach‑through claim attempts to cover basic research or downstream products discovered through a screening or identification method (claims for products or uses when experimental screening data is provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as attempting to capture value before a full invention; treated as an exception to normal claiming practice and often denied (example: reach‑through claim for Celebrex was refused). Such claims are viewed skeptically as overreaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A signal claim is a claim for an electromagnetic signal that embodies information (e.g., 'An electromagnetic signal carrying computer‑readable instructions...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S., transitory signal claims are not statutory subject matter per In re Nuijten (signals not patentable). A petition for rehearing and certiorari were denied. In contrast, the EPO's Board of Appeal has held that the EPC does not as such exclude patentability of signals (decision T 533/09); national practices vary. The page notes the legal tensions and differing treatment by jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swiss‑type claim (Swiss‑type of use claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe, a Swiss‑type claim is a claim format used to cover the first, second, or subsequent medical use (method of treatment not directly patentable under EPC) by claiming 'Use of substance X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of condition Y'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Was a workaround under earlier EPC practice to protect second medical uses; the EPO Enlarged Board decision G 2/08 (and later changes to EPC Article 54(5)) affected the availability of Swiss‑type claims for second medical use. National practices differ: some countries allowed Swiss‑type claims where methods of treatment are not patentable. The page explains the legal rationale and that EPO/UPC jurisprudence changed the role of Swiss‑type claims.
